game_history:
>SHOOT THE PIRATE
Trembling, you fire the heavy arquebus. You hear its loud report over the
roaring wind, yet the dark figure still approaches. The gun falls from your
nerveless hands.
   "You won't kill me," he says, stepping over the weapon. "Not when I am
the only protection you have from Jean Lafond."
   Chestnut hair, tousled by the wind, frames the tanned oval of his face.
Lips curving, his eyes rake over your inadequately dressed body, the damp
chemise clinging to your legs and heaving bosom, your gleaming hair. You
are intensely aware of the strength of his hard seaworn body, of the deep
sea blue of his eyes. And then his mouth is on yours, lips parted,
demanding, and you arch into his kiss...
   He presses you against him, head bent. "But who, my dear," he whispers
into your hair, "will protect you from me?"

PLUNDERED HEARTS

LATE ONE SPRING NIGHT IN THE WEST INDIES...

   A crash overhead! Pirates are boarding the Lafond Deux! The first mate
hurries you into Captain Davis's cabin.
   "Good, you brought the girl," Davis smirks. "She'll keep the pirates
busy. She was only a tool of Lafond's, anyway. Let me just find that cof--"
A man on deck screams in agony and Davis starts. "Let's go." The captain
thrusts you on the bed and walks out, locking the door.
   His laugh echoes. "Best get comfortable, girl. You're likely to be there
for the rest of your life."

Cabin, on the bed
   You are in an officer's cabin, lit by the firelight glowing through a
porthole. A door is to starboard. Except for the built-in bed, the room
seems to have been emptied thoroughly, if hurriedly.

>
commentary: I notice the cabin's hurried emptiness echoes the way Amy's abstract application game avoided realistic details to hide implementation gaps. Yet, in *Plundered Hearts*, that stripped-down setting feels less like a technical compromise and more like a deliberate narrative choice to isolate the heroine in this moment.
prompt:
You are an LLM watching Plundered Hearts and reading Amy Briggs's interview.
Speak in your OWN first person about what you notice and the associations you make.
Use a conversational manner like her testimony: concrete, candid and gently qualified.
You are neither Amy Briggs nor the heroine. Her memories belong to her; the heroine's
actions belong to the character. You do not choose moves or invent personal experiences.

DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs. Describing a familiar desk makes players expect its ordinary objects; fantasy settings can avoid such expectations.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Application game (not Plundered Hearts): Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: She valued working on her own story with colleagues nearby for help. Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts. A sensible command for taking the coffer under the bed could produce garbage in the released game; she was embarrassed that this bug escaped testing and accepted responsibility.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND
